ai-at-work.title: OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users, new data indicates
ai-at-work.excerpt: Businesses are willing to flop back and forth as each lab releases new models, volatility that should give both companies' investors pause about how "sticky" enterprise AI spending really is.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: OpenAI is pulling ahead of Anthropic in the race for business customers, according to new adoption data, though both companies are seeing customers switching between their tools as new models drop. This matters because it shows enterprise AI spending is still highly unstable, which means your organization's AI strategy needs flexibility built in rather than bet-the-farm commitment to one vendor. After thirty years watching tech cycles, I can tell you the "stickiness" problem is really just another word for "nobody actually knows what they're doing yet," and that's fine, but pretending otherwise will cost you money.

ai-at-work.title: VentureBeat names Rob Strechay as its first Lead Analyst, expanding its enterprise AI research push
ai-at-work.excerpt: Rob Strechay, until recently managing director and principal analyst at theCUBE Research, has joined VentureBeat as our first Lead Analyst and a founding analyst of VentureBeat Research. His arrival i
ai-at-work.dwp_take: VentureBeat hired Rob Strechay from theCUBE Research as its first Lead Analyst to beef up enterprise AI research coverage aimed at technical decision-makers like CIOs and CTOs. This matters because digital workplace pros need trustworthy voices cutting through the AI hype to tell them what actually works in their environments. Strechay's got solid credentials, but let's see if VentureBeat can resist the temptation to turn "enterprise AI research" into the same breathless cheerleading everyone else does.

ai-at-work.title: Google’s attempt to buy Spirit Airlines’ data might come unstuck
ai-at-work.excerpt: Google LLC’s artificial intelligence researchers had been salivating at the prospect of getting their hands on a trove of business data acquired from the defunct airline Spirit Airlines Inc. in an auc
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google tried to buy Spirit Airlines' bankruptcy data for ten million dollars to train AI models, but the deal is now facing legal challenges in court. Digital workplace pros need to care because this signals how aggressively tech companies are hunting for real-world operational data, and it matters whether that data gets protected or auctioned off. Here's the thing: if Google loses this fight, it won't stop them from finding another airline's data pile. It'll just make them more creative about it.

ai-at-work.title: Astromech raises $20M to build a biological operating system that can forecast evolutionary change
ai-at-work.excerpt: An artificial intelligence startup called Astromech that’s developing models that can predict biological change has raised $20 million in funding, lifting its valuation to $3.8 billion. The round was
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Astromech just grabbed $20 million to build AI models that predict how biological systems evolve and change over time. For digital workplace folks, this matters because understanding adaptive systems is exactly what we need to build workplaces that actually evolve instead of breaking every time we add a new tool. The irony is thick here: we're funding billion-dollar startups to predict biological change while most organizations still can't predict what their own employees need next quarter.

tools-tech.title: Why replacing staff with AI backfires - and 5 ways smart leaders generate real value instead
tools-tech.excerpt: Three-quarters of organizations have found AI layoffs cost more than they saved, and as many as nine in 10 companies would rethink them given the chance.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Most companies that fired people to deploy AI discovered it actually cost them more money than keeping those people around, with up to 90% saying they'd reverse the decision if they could. This matters because digital workplace leaders are now facing real pressure to prove AI adoption doesn't automatically mean headcount reduction, and they need better business cases to justify implementations. The irony is thick here: turns out humans are still pretty good at context, relationships, and not breaking things when you ask them to do their jobs, which AI can definitely help with but apparently cannot replace without burning cash.

tools-tech.title: The best and worst AI for your privacy, ranked - and how each handles your data
tools-tech.excerpt: Incogni researchers analyze 13 AI platforms and the potential risks they each pose to your privacy. The larger the platform, the bigger the risk - with one exception.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Researchers ranked 13 AI platforms by their privacy risks, finding that bigger platforms generally pose bigger threats to your data, with one notable outlier breaking the pattern. This matters because your employees are already using these tools for work whether you've approved them or not, and if they're syncing company data to the cloud, you've got a compliance headache waiting to happen. The irony is thick here: we've spent decades building security infrastructures to protect data, and now half your workforce is casually uploading sensitive stuff to whatever AI chatbot just went viral.

tools-tech.title: Apple to OpenAI: Go to your room
tools-tech.excerpt: Apple’s latest filing in its ongoing fight with OpenAI makes it sound as if Apple legal is so frustrated at the arguments the AI firm is making that it’s begun swatting them away like a parent might d
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple sued OpenAI and is apparently winning the argument phase so decisively that their legal filings read like a parent telling a toddler to stop talking. This matters because it signals that even AI darlings face serious intellectual property and competitive challenges, and workplace tech leaders need to understand the legal landscape around AI tools they're considering. Watching a trillion-dollar company basically tell an AI firm to sit down and be quiet is oddly satisfying, honestly.

digital-culture.title: Exclusive: This $100 million startup wants to give companies AI employees
digital-culture.excerpt: At the San Francisco-based startup Anything AI, there’s a robust team that seems like any fast-growing startup’s organizational chart. There’s Emma, who investigates reported bugs across logs, databas
digital-culture.dwp_take: A $100 million San Francisco startup called Anything AI is building AI agents designed to function as actual employees handling real work like bug investigation, operations planning, brand management, and inbox triage. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to seriously think about where AI fits in their real organizational structures instead of just bolting it onto existing systems as a tool. Honestly, naming your AI employees like they're characters from a British sitcom is either visionary or a sign we're all living in some weird corporate fanfiction, but either way these things are coming whether we're ready or not.

digital-culture.title: Perimenopause, menopause symptoms may cost employees nearly 35 workdays a year
digital-culture.excerpt: Perimenopause and menopause, normal transitions that impact people who menstruate as hormone levels begin to fall off, might be more disruptive to the work lives of those experiencing symptoms than pr
digital-culture.dwp_take: A new study estimates that perimenopause and menopause symptoms cost employees roughly 35 workdays annually through reduced productivity and absences. This matters because digital workplace leaders need to stop treating health accommodations as nice-to-haves and recognize them as basic operational reality that affects a huge chunk of your workforce. If we can spend billions on standing desks and coffee machines, we can probably figure out flexible schedules and temperature controls without breaking a sweat, except for the people already doing that involuntarily.

digital-culture.title: Why do companies care which days you work from home?
digital-culture.excerpt: Bank of America has announced a unique change to its hybrid work policy: it will prohibit employees from working remotely on consecutive days. Starting on September 14, Bank of America staff in hybrid
digital-culture.dwp_take: Bank of America is forcing hybrid workers to split their remote days so employees can't work from home on consecutive days, starting September 14th. This matters because it reveals what companies actually prioritize when they talk about "collaboration" and "flexibility": real estate utilization and control, not employee preference. Honestly, if your collaboration strategy depends on forcing people to commute twice as often instead of building better async processes and communication tools, you're solving the wrong problem.

digital-culture.title: How to get your attention span back
digital-culture.excerpt: We live in a world of distraction. In the time it took me to write this sentence, I got a new email alert on my computer, two new DMs, and an alert on my phone that my Duolingo streak is in jeopardy.
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company published a piece about reclaiming focus in a world of constant digital notifications and interruptions. This matters because digital workplace professionals spend their days drowning in alerts and competing priorities, which directly tanks productivity and burnout rates. Here's the thing though: the real issue isn't your broken brain, it's that your tools and culture are designed to keep you fragmented, and no productivity hack fixes that until someone actually changes how work gets communicated.

industry-news.dwp_take: Google and Apple are both asking a grand for their flagship phones, but they're betting on different things to justify it: camera smarts versus ecosystem lock-in. For anyone managing corporate device programs, this comparison matters because your choice shapes everything from deployment costs to support headaches to whether your workforce can actually collaborate seamlessly. Here's the reality: you're not picking the better phone, you're picking which company's particular flavor of vendor lock-in bothers you less.

industry-news.title: Windows 11 Hotpatching Explained: How Much Does It Really Reduce Reboots?
industry-news.excerpt: Windows 11 hotpatching can install security updates without reboots. Learn who qualifies, how the update cycle works, and what IT teams should expect. The post Windows 11 Hotpatching Explained: How Mu
industry-news.dwp_take: Microsoft released hotpatching for Windows 11, which installs security patches without forcing a system reboot. That said, I've seen Microsoft promise frictionless updates before, so I'll believe hotpatching delivers on its hype when I see actual enterprise numbers showing fewer 2am calls to the help desk.

industry-news.excerpt: Galaxy Watch9 costs $20 less than Pixel Watch 5, but phone compatibility, battery life, and access to health features may matter more. The post Pixel Watch 5 vs Galaxy Watch9: Price, Battery, Features
industry-news.dwp_take: Google's Pixel Watch 5 and Samsung's Galaxy Watch9 are being compared on price, battery life, and features, with the Galaxy Watch9 coming in $20 cheaper. For digital workplace managers thinking about wearable device strategies, this matters because battery life and ecosystem compatibility directly impact employee adoption and support costs. industry-news.title: How to Quiz Yourself With ChatGPT and Check the Answers
industry-news.excerpt: A better ChatGPT quiz starts with a tighter prompt, a clear difficulty level, and independent checks when the answer actually matters. The post How to Quiz Yourself With ChatGPT and Check the Answers
industry-news.dwp_take: ChatGPT can generate quiz questions for self-study, but only if you write prompts carefully and verify the answers yourself because the AI hallucinates with confidence. This matters because knowledge workers are increasingly using AI for learning and development, and bad information dressed up as a quiz is worse than no quiz at all. Here's the thing: if you're relying on an AI to both ask and answer your own questions, you're not learning, you're just playing a very expensive guessing game.
